records.name: Sabina
records.facts_used: Sabina: The family is based on Latin Sabina, the feminine of Sabinus. It referred to the Sabines, a people of ancient Italy. This is an ethnic designation in the name’s history, not a statement about a modern bearer’s nationality or personal qualities. The Latvian Language Agency gives the exact rendering Sabina → Sabina, citing page 145 of a 2015 manual. This dated record illustrates transmission between languages; it is not a first birth registration or proof of one borrowing route in every family.

records.name: Sarma
records.facts_used: Sarma: Sarma is a Latvian name from sarma, hoarfrost: white ice crystals on surfaces. Its base belongs to Latvian rather than a similar-sounding foreign name. The natural image does not determine a bearer’s personality or the season of her birth. Siliņš’s dictionary dates the use of Sarma: 1507. Its calendar year is 1908. This records use of the particular name in Latvia. The entry cannot automatically be transferred to similar spellings or treated as the moment the entire name family originated.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Catalogue gives1507record/calendar1908; no inventor or modern naming mechanism inferred from old attestation.

records.name: Gratas
records.facts_used: Gratas: Lithuanian Gratas is explained through Latin gratus, pleasing or welcome. The link is to a Latin word rather than an accidentally similar Lithuanian syllable. The historical adjective helps explain the personal name’s formation, without promising a person’s character. The 1964 calendar reprinted in Salys’s 1983 volume gives Gratas on 5 December. This is a concrete printed example of the form’s use. Its position in the historical calendar need not match every modern calendar and is not the name’s invention date.

records.name: Gracija
records.facts_used: Gracija: Gracija belongs to the Gracia/Gratia group. The Lithuanian guide points to Spanish gracia, grace; the family’s earlier lexical base is Latin gratia. Transmission through languages forms part of its history without proving one route in every family. The Dictionary of Medieval Names records related Latin Gracia in France in 1287. This documented example shows the family in use before the modern Lithuanian spelling. It is not the first Lithuanian registration of exact Gracija.

records.name: Eimintas
records.facts_used: Eimintas: The Lithuanian guide identifies ei- from eiti, to go, and mint- from minti, mintis, to think or thought. Pakerys’s study directly links the ei- group to eiti. This is a linguistic analysis of a compound name; the stems need not be turned into an invented full sentence. Printed page 92 of Pakerys’s 2010 article gives exact Eimintas with an asterisk. In the notation he uses, that marks a name recently formed and brought into use in the twentieth century rather than attested in ancient records. It documents modern name formation without identifying an individual inventor.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Original PDF5printed92 exact Eĩmintas; PDF2printed89 footnote1 defines asterisk as twentieth-century newlyformed, not unrecorded hypothetical ancient reconstruction. Original spelling was visually checked with accent Eĩmintas; normalized calendar spelling is Eimintas.
